title: Wayseeking Mind
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: Shuko Edie Norton shares that through their Zen practice, they've come to understand that true fulfillment and purpose come from being fully engaged with the present moment, rather than seeking external validation or attachment to specific relationships. They've let go of attachments and ego, recognizing that even long-term practitioners can struggle with partiality, but can work towards greater wholeness through practice and self-reflection. By embracing the present moment, they've found a sense of peace and relief from suffering, allowing them to cultivate a deeper understanding of reality and find liberation from long-held beliefs about themselves.

sentences.text: Two or three of you really don't have to be here, but if you want to stay you get extra credit.
They've heard it in Vancouver before, so I'm happy to be here among you.
The Way Seeking Mind talk, as you probably know, in fact I can't quite see Tim, so I'll move back a little bit.
My talk, as you know, is to tell the story of one's practice and one's life, and how it came to Zen.
I'm going to do that briefly, but mostly what I want to focus on today is the Way Seeking I have been doing this past year, studying my mind and dealing with it.
I want to talk about the mind and how it seems to work, and about my mind and how this year I've experienced some liberation from some long-held but no longer useful beliefs about myself.
Excuse my voice, I hope that the tea will smooth it out.
Over my 37 years in Zen practice, I have been fascinated by how Zazen has enabled me from time to time to intervene in the various states of mental stuckness that my mind gets me into.
How Zazen mind has helped me to free myself from my ordinary mind's steel trap.

On several occasions in my life, after months and even years of struggling with some problem in relationship, without being able to solve it, I finally, in desperation, sat down in Zazen and said, "Okay, I'm not going to get up until I get to the bottom of this."
Somewhat like what the Buddha did under the Bodhi tree, but not nearly with such great results, of course.
What I've discovered is that the focus and also the spaciousness of Zazen mind allows me to get insight into this problem and find a way to solve it.
So I've been really interested in how it can help me and have relied upon it for these many years.
I want to tell you a little bit about the nature of my practice and how I came to Zen next.
I think I can characterize my practice over the years as applied Buddhism.
I've always looked for and found a practical use for what I was learning and understanding about Buddhism.

Although I studied some primary texts, such as the Lotus Sutra and the Heart Sutra, I've not been drawn to the mysteries of Koan stories or to the Pali texts as much as I have been to writers and teachers who can explain Buddhist concepts to me.

I've tried to apply Buddhist concepts in my daily life to face what's really going on, to not flee from what's going on, to understand how we are not separate and how reality itself is dependently co-arising.

I've had my share of challenges in my life for this application of Buddhist ideas: divorce, suicide of my husband, being a single mother, educating myself for three major career changes, and relocating my home after 40 years in one place.
Throughout my adult life, my struggle to understand Buddhism has always been exciting.
As I've looked back over the years of my Zen practice, a theme has emerged around the big question of home leaving, the obligation and opportunity that Dogen says we have when we take the precepts.

I see that to this question of home leaving over the years, I've responded in two ways: first with hesitation, and then with risk taking, and then with hesitation again, and then with taking another risk.

So I want to talk today about how the events of my life and my halting movement through them, all the while struggling to learn and apply Buddhist understandings, has led me finally to leave home in a way I never expected to do.
Hesitation and risk taking are part of my natural repertoire of behaviors.

I'm an introvert, I'm studious and cautious with a tendency toward fearfulness, and initially uncertain about the rightness of my views, and needing to reflect and feel some certainty about my plan before I act.
Plus, I realize now that I failed as a young person to develop much self-confidence, so I've been hesitant in that regard as well.
Hesitation and risk taking as life and practice themes appear throughout my talk, but first let me tell you a little bit more about home leaving.
Home leaving has been a major theme in my [unclear: "stay in life"] several times over the years, because several times over the years I have seriously considered being ordained as a priest.
But each time I just couldn't do it because I never felt I could fully commit to making the sangha my first priority, as I thought I would need to do.
And of course, deciding not to take that step, I've always wondered if my practice would have been better if I had.
So I give myself a bad time.
I think something like home leaving even appealed to me when I was a teenager and going to a Presbyterian church with my parents.
The minister there gave really good talks about how to apply Christian beliefs.
I fantasized that maybe I could take up the religious life.
Well, this was back in the early 1950s and it was a rare young girl who was thinking or would become a minister.
But I thought entering the religious life for me would be marrying a minister.
And I knew a really cute boy who was going to become a minister.
I'm glad that has changed a lot in our society.
Although in high school I was genuinely spiritual, once I went to college I was cowed by my intellectual and atheistic religion.
In my heart I didn't really believe this, but I lacked the self-confidence to challenge that prevailing skepticism.
So sadly I did nothing about my spirit for almost 20 years.
It was only as I was approaching 40 and in a very difficult marriage that I discovered Buddhism.
I was struggling with what I later came to understand was my husband's alcoholism.
Ironically he turned out to be both my demon and my angel, for he led me to Zen.
To help me calm down from my agitation and anxiety about his behavior and to take the heat off of him, he said, "Why don't you read some Zen?"
I read Alan Watts' The Way of Zen and I took a full year reading it and puzzling over the strange paradoxical statements that were in that book.

Gradually over the next year I read some other books, among them Philip Caplow's The Three Pillars of Zen, where I found at the back some illustrated instructions about how to sit zazen, which I tried at home, but felt I didn't really know how to do.
Just then I read in the paper that there was going to be a Zen Buddhism class being taught at the local community college.
With a surge of excitement, my heart in my throat, I signed up for it.
What was I doing, I thought.
The first evening of the class, a slender Japanese man with a shaved head and a flowing robe swept into the room and I was just entranced.
Even though I could understand only a little of what he said in his kind of broken English, I found him magical.
This was Kobun Chino Otogawa, just three years in the United States on the invitation of Suzuki Roshi to come and help [unclear: "Stardom"] Tassajara.
He became the teacher at Haiku Zendo in Los Altos, California.
He became my root teacher.
I was a devoted student of Kobun's and an active member of Haiku Zendo.
Later, at the next location that we had, which was called Kannon Do, Kobun helped me through a time of major crisis in my life, my husband's alcoholism and eventual suicide.
A year or so after that period, which was about four years, in which I received the precepts from Kobun, he shocked all of us by telling us he no longer wanted to be the teacher at his center.
And we should all go off and practice on our own.
He was leaving to become an itinerant teacher.
Well, this was a big shock.
Some people kind of refused to let him go.
They just kept calling him and trying to see him and so forth.
But I realized that he really wanted to leave us.
To honor that, I accepted, as painful as it was, that he was going away.
He had helped me so enormously through my life challenges in the previous couple of years that I felt I really needed to support him in what he wanted to do.
So in retrospect, though, I still honor Kobun as my original dear teacher.
His leaving actually did leave me wandering a bit.
In a sense, homeless in my practice for quite a number of years.
My next practice at Kannon Do, which was Haiku Zendo, which was in a home garage, was closed.
And we moved to another couple of centers.
Kannon Do in Mountain View was the one that I went to.
I practiced there for 10 years.
I was on the board there for several years, and I facilitated a visioning and mission statement development for a year there with the sangha.
Les Kaye was the priest there and still is actually.
He was a good teacher, but he never somehow became my teacher.
So after 10 years of practicing there, I was feeling parched for teachings that spoke more directly to me.
I started searching for another teacher.
Eventually, I met Reb Anderson at Green Gulch and found his Dharma talks really good and helpful to me.
I asked him if I could study with him and he said yes.
But then I could never work it out so I could go up there very often.
It was two hours from where I lived.
I was working full time.
I had my younger son at home and it just didn't work out for me to travel up there often.
During these years, about 15 or so, I didn't go to many sesshins.
I didn't go to any long sesshins.
Because I had a serious back problem, I was convinced I would not be able to sit for long periods.
So I didn't accumulate much experience in intensive practice as would have been the case for a serious student such as I was.
I did one or two day retreats.
But it was many years before I ventured into a seven day retreat or sesshin.
Since then, I found I could do it and I've done many of them.
So it took me a long time to get over that.
In 1973, I had the chance to go to Japan to teach English and to live in Okayama where there's a famous Rinzai temple, Sogenji.
It's a training temple for European and American [unclear: "sands students"].
In the summer, I lived there for five weeks.
Throughout the year, I went there on weekends and for sesshins.
During the summer, in that time when I was in residence, I followed their pretty rigorous schedule.
Now this was a big challenge for me to go and live in place.
I didn't know whether I would be able to do it actually.
It still kind of astonishes me as I look back over this time to realize that almost 20 years into my practice, I still didn't have a lot of confidence about it.
It takes some of us a really long time.
I didn't know if I was up to the schedule.
I didn't know if I could understand what was happening.
For the first couple of weeks, it was painful physically.
I very gradually caught on.
And then it was really easy.
Due to the big risk I felt I was taking for the first time, some confidence in my practice in Buddhism.

After a year in Japan, I returned to California and eventually found my way back to Reb, who by now was no longer [unclear: "avid"] at San Francisco Center and was teaching more widely, more publicly at weekend retreats.
Again, I found his teaching enormously helpful.
He so clearly explained many, many concepts that I had been confused about for years.
Looking back again, I realized that I was more or less untutored during the first 20 years of my practice.
There weren't many book resources available early on in my practice.
While Kobun gave Dharma talks, I really didn't understand most of what he said.
I just was happy to be in his presence.
Then later with Les Kaye, he taught mostly about zazen and did that very well, but didn't teach from text very much.
So I didn't have much Buddhist education, just zazen pretty much.
So when I got to Reb's teaching, it was a huge boost for me.
I didn't have much contact with him other than three or four retreats a year.
But I managed to benefit greatly from those.
Finally, in the year 2000, I signed up for and went to the three-week winter practice period at Green Gulch.
It was a wonderful experience all around.

And because it had been so long since I'd been a Kobun student by that time, I asked Reb if he would give me the precepts a second time. [unclear: "He, for the first time to me, for it to receive him a second time."] And he agreed to do that.
He gave me a new Dharma name, which is now still my name, Zaren Shinge, which means sitting lotus, profound understanding.
Meanwhile, I was planning to move back to the Northwest where I had grown up.
I was thinking of Seattle, where I have friends.
However, at the Green Gulch retreat, a student from Whatcom County told me about Bellingham and the fact that Norman was coming up here regularly and that there was a good Zen group.
So I thought, well, that might be something worth looking into.
On a visit to Seattle later that year, I came on up to Bellingham and looked things over and said, "Yeah, I think this is the place for me."
So I went home, sold my house, and was up here in two months' time.
Can you imagine?
That was when the market was hot, I can tell you.
So this is another example of my periodic risk taking.
On moving to Bellingham, I joined our group here and got involved.
I attended retreats when Norman came to town.
My problem with home leaving was still nagging at me, home leaving in the Buddhist sense.
I told Norman about my ambivalence and regret about never having taken priest ordination.
I also told him about my interest in being involved in my new community.
He suggested that I might think of myself as a monk in the world and apply my Zen practice in my volunteer work here.
I took his suggestion and have focused on service to the community in the past seven years, working as a hospice volunteer, working in the neighborhoods and on city-wide boards and commissions.
So I was very grateful for his idea of practice in the world, that I've had some challenges in my life, as I think most of us have.
The challenge in recent years has again had to do with home leaving.
Perhaps reminiscent of Kobun's leaving us back in the 1970s, I have now experienced home leaving in terms of my relationship with my two sons.
They are now in their late 40s and early 50s with very intense and busy lives, as most people are at that age.
I raised them pretty much on my own, at first while married to an alcoholic and later myself after my husband died.
For many years I was still well connected with both of my sons, visiting them each several times a year wherever they were living: in Southern California, in Boston, in Austin, Texas, and Colorado.
But over the last six or seven years, my connection with each of them has fallen off, to my growing confusion and alarm.
Maintaining close contact has not been made any easier by the fact that one lives in Florida and the other in South Dakota.
I have stewed and worried about this loss of connection a lot.
I've talked with Norman about it, about the anguish I have felt at being less and less a part of their lives.
I've also talked to Tim and to John about this.
This past year or so, after many years of hesitation driven by my self-doubt, I spoke to each of my sons individually about my dismay at our growing separation.
I asked them to tell me if they were harboring any anger at me over incidents in their childhoods.
They claimed not.
Of course, much of their childhood, I realize, was spent in the emotional chaos of alcoholism.
There was no physical abuse, thank goodness, but there certainly was dramatic behavior and strife.
And I know that they were not unscathed.
I told them I wanted to reconnect with them, to have a good adult relationship with them.
I told them I really need them as I am growing older.
Although they were relatively gentle in their responses, they pretty much refused me.
I was shocked and depressed.
I searched myself and my life to understand what was really a heartbreaking outcome for me.
I'd always believed that I'd been a good mother, but my sons are good people, and they never got into driving their good fathers to their own children.

I observed on a recent two-week visit to my older son and his family in Florida that his life is entirely taken up with his academic career and his family, his wife and his two children, both of whom have some problems.
So I understand better now why he can't fit me into his life except only.
I also observed how much he loves his daughters, to whom he is very kind and patient.
He loves them just as much as I loved him and still do, and I sense that some of that love had to have come through me to him and to his children.
So I felt my wounded heart soften a little.

The facts of his situation relieve me somewhat of my concern that I had been the cause of the distance between us, though they don't solve the problem of the loss I feel from the continuing lack of connection with him.
In effect, I'm feeling homeless because of this loss.
But of course, like all of us students, this loss has also been an important teaching about my preferences and attachments.

As I read recently in Rodney Smith's remarkable book, Stepping Out of Self-Deception, from which I will quote again, Rodney says, *And thereby I have been suffering.* Concurrent to this unwanted alienation from my sons, I was and still am working with dying patients in hospice.
In my work there, I have witnessed that it can be very hard to give up one's life if there are unresolved issues and relationships.
One of my hospice patients was a friend of mine, and I was able to spend more intimate time with her as she approached death.
She was very brave and worked hard at accepting that her illness was terminal.
But when she discovered that she had only a few days to live, she was overcome with grief for the loss of her life.
She was reconciled to dying, but she just hadn't expected it to come so quickly.
She was in good relationship to her two children, but accepting that she would die very soon was still very painful for her.
For me, it might be all I can handle to let go of my own life without also having to reconcile my relationship with my sons.
Since dying is an event that I am now closer to than I was earlier in my life, achieving this sense of completion has taken on an urgency for me.
Furthermore, when I come to die, I do really want to feel that my life has been worthwhile.
So I have a kind of big challenge here.
About a year ago, my concern about this hit crisis pitch, alarmed that I might go to my death having failed to affect a close loving relationship with the two most important people in my life.
And therefore I won't be able to consider my life worthwhile.
I sought counseling in the form of cognitive therapy, where I examined and began to change the way I was thinking about my role and relationship to my sons.
Cognitive therapy, you may know, asks one to examine negative beliefs and substitute more realistic and constructive ones.
During several months working with my therapist, I did most of the work at home on my own, reporting to her in our sessions and getting further guidance from her as to what to do next.
At home, I wrote down my thoughts, examined why I felt the way I felt, and considered other options for my thinking.
I found I couldn't easily reframe my thinking.
I had to deal first with my resistance, my skepticism, my emotions, my grief and anger, despair, very directly before I could make any shifts in my thinking.
It was hard work, but very interesting to me that through a very intensive examination, I could change the way I thought.
Just as in those times in the past when I had used Zazen mind to address and solve an emotionally laden problem that my ordinary mind couldn't solve, I applied Zazen mind to my current problem.

Through this intensive examination, I realized that a big reason why I wanted to be closer to my sons was so that they could reassure me that I had been a good mother and therefore had led a good life.
When I saw through this false reasoning, I realized also that I needed to figure out how to feel good about my life, irrespective of my relationship to my sons.
Not an easy task, but a real and essential one, and one I had been blind to when I was unconsciously hoping my sons could do it for me.

Over a period of about four or five months, I worked intensively, examining my thinking and my self-talk, and reframing beliefs, such as the one I just mentioned, that were negative and unconstructive.
I managed to penetrate a whole network of misconceptions and negative conclusions about me.
Although this was difficult and often painful work, I was encouraged because it was pretty exciting to see my mind changing.
I began to reconstruct a more realistic view of my life and my relationship with my sons and with others.
For one thing, I came to realize that my sons and I have become quite different people from who we were when we were all more closely bound together in earlier years.
This is really no surprise when I consider it objectively, but I had never realized that before.
For another thing, I've come to the startling realization that maybe I can no longer define myself as a mother.
The one role I felt I still had...
I had given up being a mate, I had given up being a professional, being a horseback rider, a skier.
I'm still a swimmer and a yogi, but I've given up quite a number of things as I've grown older.
It came as a shock that maybe I am no longer a mother, at least in any functioning way.
I wondered how I could get to believing my life had been worthwhile if my one mainstay, motherhood, no longer pertained.
Of course, this identity crisis also brought up doubts about my Zen practice and why it had not been sufficient to sustain me through this.
Had I not been faithful enough, say, lazy, lacking commitment, belief?
Yeah, yeah, maybe yeah.
Why, after so many years of practice, was I still struggling in such a fundamental way?
Or struggling again?
Maybe I actually should have become a priest, or would I have failed at that too?
So, the self-doubt drill.
You might have had the experience of having a book, just the right book or just the right teaching, fall into your hands just when you need it most.

This has been happening to me in the past few months as I have been confronting these painful realities of my life and nature, and also as I've been preparing to be Shuso, which has been a powerful process in itself.

The Rodney Smith book that I mentioned earlier is one of the books, but there have been several others, including even a novel about the mind, that really helped me get some insight into how our minds work.

Rodney Smith says, as a way of reassuring me as I read it, *the call of the Dharma is toward the difficult, not the comfortable.* And a few pages later, *an awakened life depends upon addressing the pain of being separated from those I love most.*
Just in time, these sentences gave me solace.
He said that it's pretty common for even long-term practitioners to get stuck, to fail to push through and break out of the limitations of the ego and the mind.
It is because our mind is so invested in maintaining our sense of self that we feel separate from others.
That is, it's the thought that we're separate, and that alone, that makes us separate.
Our feeling separate has no more reality than that.
So I began to think, well, maybe I'm not so disconnected.
Again, Rodney Smith, speaking of renunciation in Dharma practice, says that what we must renounce in practice is a partial heart.
That's what keeps us from full realization or enlightenment or liberation.
It's an incomplete embrace of the moment.
I see now that my habit of hesitation has kept me from wholeheartedness a lot of times.
Smith goes on to say that what prevents us from being wholly present in the moment is our competing intentions.
Certainly being a person with many interests, I realize I've had many competing intentions in my life that have competed with my devotion to Zen practice.
Competing intentions have been at the heart of my struggle about priesthood and perhaps also characteristic of my practice generally.
I have often, though not always, had a partial heart.
So even after 37 years of practice, this is probably a fundamental reason why I've struggled to fully trust my beliefs, as I've always wanted to.
I very much regret my partial heart.
I'm even ashamed of it.
And yet I recognize it is an essential aspect of myself.
And therefore, it's what I must and do practice with.
It is a condition of being me.
Perhaps the essential pain.
Rodney goes on to say, *until there is complete dedication to being in the same place and same time as our body, our life is incomplete and irresolute.
We must understand we are not needed anywhere but now.
And our only purpose for being is here.
Spiritual fulfillment can be defined as a complete abiding in the here.*
So I ask myself, where am I now?
I am here.
I'm not with my sons and their families.
In effect, or perhaps even by definition, I am not needed there.
My life is here.
Therefore, again, perhaps by definition, this is where I am needed.
Here is where I will find liberation.
Only here.
"One who can save myself": the Buddha's admonition to us all.
Not my sons, not anyone else.
Of course, I've known this for years.
But it's only now, when I've come to feel my vulnerability to old age, sickness, and death, that I have finally understood it with my heart.

Through this crisis of identity this past year, through the hard work of therapy that I've done, through the wonderful books that I've found or that have found me when I most needed them, through my sons leaving me when I could not understand that I had to leave them.
I think I finally understand what to do.
It is by living my life wholeheartedly where I am, by continuing to learn and grow, that I will be able to die feeling my life has been worthwhile.
And even though I continue to sense a hardcore resistance within me when I think about relinquishing my sons, I do believe now that by following my heart, I will find what I need to do.
That is, by living in the present moment, I can live wholeheartedly.
It's common to think that when we grow old, even if we're healthy, we just fade away, lose interest and engagement in life.
I had expected this.
But I'm here to tell you that life can get even more interesting.
There is always more to learn and understand, and of course we know change never ceases.
Norman has said, "We're fully alive until we're not."
And maybe, as Norman has encouraged me to believe, my sons will come closer sometime in the future when their journeys allow it.
I don't count on that, but I will certainly be open and happy if that becomes a reality.
But whatever happens, I feel I now understand that in order to live fullheartedly, which is to live in my body in the present, that's what I have.

This recent experience of letting go of how things ought to be, just enough so I could see something different, has allowed me to see that my long-held preference that my sons relate to me in a way that makes me feel good about myself is the very thing that is preventing me from feeling good.
Also, I think I understand something I didn't before.
I'm thinking that maybe love flows mostly one way, from me to my sons, from my sons to their children.
My love for my sons doesn't come back directly to me as I've been expecting and hoping for, but it makes a big, wide circle.
These shifts in my understanding have helped me to accept and choose the reality that is here, not the version that I had wished for.
It thus relieved my suffering some.
Being as hard-headed as I seem to have been all my life, always wanting things the way I would, I require a pretty major crisis in order to change.
The last nine months, I have been working at changing my habitual, historical perceptions and beliefs.
My work is not done.
I have a ways to go before I no longer wish things could be different.
But I am certain that I would not have been able to make any of this shift without Zazen and the calm center and suspension of the habitual thought that it offers.
I am grateful and thrilled, actually, that at my advancing age, my mind is capable of such an important shift.

Although the struggle I've been having in my old age might be discouraging for you to hear, if you are looking forward to a peaceful decline, I hope you too will be encouraged that you can count on Zazen throughout your life to lead you where you need to go.

In my heart I didn't really believe this, but I lacked the self-confidence to challenge that prevailing skepticism. So sadly I did nothing about my spirit for almost 20 years. It was only as I was approaching 40 and in a very difficult marriage that I discovered Buddhism. I was struggling with what I later came to understand was my husband's alcoholism. And ironically he turned out to be both my demon and my angel, for he led me to Zen. To help me calm down from my agitation and anxiety about his behavior and to take the heat off of him, he said, why don't you read some Zen? And I read Alan Watts' The Way of Zen and I took a full year reading it and puzzling over the strange paradoxical statements that were in that book.

Gradually over the next year I read some other books, among them Philip Caplow's The Three Pillars of Zen, where I found at the back some illustrated instructions about how to sit zazen, which I tried at home, but felt I didn't really know how to do. Just then I read in the paper that there was going to be a Zen Buddhism class being taught at the local community college. With a surge of excitement in my throat, my heart in my throat, I signed up for it. What was I doing, I thought. The first evening of the class, a slender Japanese man with a shaved head and a flowing robe swept into the room and I was just entranced. Even though I could understand only a little of what he said in his kind of broken English, I found him magical. This was Kobun Chino Otogawa just three years in the United States on the invitation of Suzuki Roshi to come and help Stardom Tosahara.

And he became the teacher at Haikusendo in Los Altos, California. He became my root teacher. I was a devoted student of Koban's and an active member of Haikusendo. And later at the next location that we had, which was called Kanendo, Koban helped me through a time of major crisis in my life, my husband's alcoholism and eventual suicide. A year or so after that period, which was about four years, in which I received the precepts from Koban, he shocked all of us by telling us he no longer wanted to be the teacher at his center. And we should all go off and practice on our own.

He was leaving to become an itinerant teacher. Well, this was a big shock. And some people kind of refused to let him go. They just kept calling him and trying to see him and so forth. But I realized that he really wanted to leave us. And so to honor that, I accepted, as painful as it was, that he was going away. He had helped me so enormously through my life challenges in the previous couple of years that I felt I really needed to support him in what he wanted to do.

So in retrospect, though, I still honor Koban as my original dear teacher. His leaving actually did leave me wandering a bit. In a sense, homeless in my practice for quite a number of years. My next practice at Kanando, which was Haikusendo, which was in a home garage, was closed. And we moved to another couple of centers. Kanando and Mountain View was the one that I went to. And I practiced there for 10 years. I was on the board there for several years.

And I facilitated a visioning and mission statement development for a year. There with the sangha. And Les Kaye was the priest there and still is actually. He was a good teacher, but he never somehow became my teacher. So after 10 years of practicing there, I was feeling parched for teachings that spoke more directly to me. And so I started searching for another teacher. Eventually, I met Reb Anderson at Green Gulch and found his Dharma talks really good and helpful to me. I asked him if I could study with him and he said yes.

But then I could never work it out so I could go up there very often. It was two hours from where I lived. I was working full time. I had my younger son at home and it just didn't work out for me to travel up there often. During these years, about 15 or so, I didn't go to many sesshins. I didn't go to any long sesshins. Because I had a serious back problem, I was convinced I would not be able to sit for long periods. So I didn't accumulate much experience in intensive practice as would have been the case for a serious student such as I was.

I did one or two day retreats. But it was many years before I ventured into a seven day retreat or sesshin. And then, since then, I found I could do it and I've done many of them. So it took me a long time to get over that. In 1973, I had the chance to go to Japan to teach English and to live in Okayama where there's a famous Rinzai temple, Sogenji. It's a training temple for European and American sands students. In the summer, I lived there for five weeks. And throughout the year, I went there on weekends and for sesshins.

And during the summer, in that time when I was in residence, I followed their pretty rigorous schedule. Now this was a big challenge for me to go and live in place. I didn't know whether I would be able to do it actually. And it still kind of astonishes me as I look back over this time to realize that almost 20 years into my practice, I still didn't have a lot of confidence about it. It takes some of us a really long time. I didn't know if I was up to the schedule. I didn't know if I could understand what was happening.

And for the first couple of weeks, it was painful physically. And I was very gradually caught on. And then it was really easy. Due to the big risk I felt I was taking for the first time, some confidence in my practice in Buddhism. After a year in Japan, I returned to California and eventually found my way back to Rev, who by now was no longer avid at San Francisco Center and was teaching more widely, more publicly at weekend retreats. Again, I found his teaching enormously helpful. He so clearly explained many, many concepts that I had been confused about for years.

Looking back again, I realized that I was more or less untutored during the first 20 years of my practice. There weren't many book resources available early on in my practice. And while Kobun gave Dharma talks, I really didn't understand most of what he said. And I just was happy to be in his presence. And then later with Les K, he taught mostly about Sazen and did that very well, but didn't teach from text very much. So I didn't have much Buddhist education, just Sazen pretty much. So when I got to Rev's teaching, it was a huge boost for me. I didn't have much contact with him other than that three or four retreats a year.

But I managed to benefit greatly from those. Finally, in the year 2000, I signed up for and went to the three-week winter practice period at Green Gorge. It was a wonderful experience all around. And because I've been so long since I've been a Kobun student by that time, I asked Rev if he would give me the precepts a second time. He, for the first time to me, for it to receive him a second time. And he agreed to do that. And he gave me a new Dharma name, which is now still my name, Zaren Shinge, which means sitting lotus, profound understanding. Meanwhile, I was planning to move back to the Northwest where I had grown up.

And I was thinking of Seattle, where I have friends. However, at the Green Gorge retreat, a student from Watkin County told me about Bellingham and the fact that Norman was coming up here regularly and that there was a good Zen group. So I thought, well, that might be something worth looking into. So on a visit to Seattle that year, later that year, I came on up to Bellingham and looked things over and said, yeah, I think this is the place for me. So I went home, sold my house, and was up here in two months' time. Can you imagine? That was when the market was hot, I can tell you.

And so this is another example of my periodic risk taking. On moving to Bellingham, I joined our group here and got involved. And I attended retreats when Norman came to town. My problem with home leaving was still nagging at me, home leaving in the Buddhist sense. And I told Norman about my ambivalence and regret about never having taken priest ordination. I also told him about my interest in being involved in my new community. He suggested that I might think of myself as a monk in the world and apply my Zen practice in my volunteer work here. I took his suggestion and have focused on service to the community in the past seven years,

working as a hospice volunteer, working in the neighborhoods and on city-wide boards and commissions. So I was very grateful for his idea of practice in the world, that I've had some challenges in my life, as I think most of us have. The challenge in recent years has again had to do with home leaving. Perhaps reminiscent of Cobens leaving us back in the 1970s, I have now experienced home leaving in terms of my relationship with my two sons. They are now in their late 40s and early 50s with very intense and busy lives, as most people are at that age. I raised them pretty much on my own, at first while married to an alcoholic and later myself after my husband died.

For many years I was still well connected with both of my sons, visiting them each several times a year wherever they were living, in Southern California, in Boston, in Austin, Texas and Colorado. But over the last six or seven years, my connection with them, each of them has fallen off to my growing confusion and alarm. Maintaining close contact has not been made any easier by the fact that one lives in Florida and the other in South Dakota. I have stewed and worried about this loss of connection a lot. I've talked with Norman about it, about the anguish I have felt and being less and less a part of their lives. I've also talked to Tim and to John about this.

This past year or so, after many years of hesitation driven by my self-doubt, I spoke to each of my sons individually about my dismay at our growing separation. I asked them to tell me if they were harboring any anger at me over incidents in their childhoods. They claimed not. Of course, much of their childhood, I realize, was spent in the emotional chaos of alcoholism. And there was no physical abuse, thank goodness, but there certainly was dramatic behavior and strife. And I know that they were not unscathed. I told them I wanted to reconnect with them, to have a good adult relationship with them.

I told them I really need them as I am growing older. Although they were relatively gentle in their responses, they pretty much refused me. I was shocked and depressed. I searched myself and my life to understand what was really a heartbreaking outcome for me. I'd always believed that I'd been a good mother, but my sons are good people, and they never got into driving their good fathers to their own children. I observed on a recent two-week visit to my older son and his family in Florida that his life is entirely taken up with his academic career and his family, his wife and his two children,

both of whom have some problems. So I understand better now why he can't fit me into his life except only. I also observed how much he loves his daughters, to whom he is very kind and patient. He loves them just as much as I loved him and still do, and I sense that some of that love had to have come through me to him and to his children. So I felt my wounded heart soften a little. The facts of his situation relieve me somewhat of my concern that I had been the cause of the distance between us, though they don't solve the problem of the loss I feel from the continuing lack of connection with him.

In effect, my feeling homeless because of this loss. But of course, like all of us in students, this loss has also been an important teaching about my preferences and attachments. As I read recently in Rodney Smith's remarkable book, Stepping Out of Self-Deception, from which I will quote again, Rodney says, And thereby I have been suffering. Concurrent to this unwanted alienation from my sons,

I was and still am working with dying patients in hospice. In my work there, I have witnessed that can be very hard to give up one's life if there are unresolved issues and relationships. One of my hospice patients was a friend of mine, And I was able to spend more intimate time with her as she approached death. She was very brave and worked hard at accepting that her illness was terminal. But when she discovered that she had only a few days to live, she was overcome with grief for the loss of her life. She was reconciled to dying, but she just hadn't expected it to come so quickly. She was in good relationship to her two children,

but accepting that she would die very soon was still very painful for her. For me, it might be all I can handle to let go of my own life without also having to reconcile my relationship with my sons. Since dying is an event that I am now closer to than I was earlier in my life, achieving this sense of completion has taken on an urgency for me. Furthermore, when I come to die, I do really want to feel that my life has been worthwhile. So I have a kind of big challenge here. About a year ago, my concern about this hit crisis pitch alarmed that I might go to my death having failed to affect a close loving relationship with the two most important people in my life.

And therefore I won't be able to consider my life worthwhile. I sought counseling in the form of cognitive therapy, where I examined and began to change the way I was thinking about my role and relationship to my sons. Cognitive therapy, you may know, asks one to examine negative beliefs and substitute more realistic and constructive ones. During several months working with my therapist, I did most of the work at home on my own, reporting to her in our sessions and getting further guidance from her as to what to do next. At home, I wrote down my thoughts, examined why I felt the way I felt, and considered other options for my thinking.

I found I couldn't easily reframe my thinking. I had to deal first with my resistance, my skepticism, my emotions, my grief and anger, despair, very directly before I could make any shifts in my thinking. It was hard work, but very interesting to me that through a very intensive examination, I could change the way I thought. Just as in those times in the past when I had used Zazen mind to address and solve an emotionally laden problem that my ordinary mind couldn't solve, I applied Zazen mind to my current problem. Through this intensive examination, I realized that a big reason why I wanted to be closer to my sons

was so that they could reassure me that I had been a good mother and therefore had led a good life. When I saw through this false reasoning, I realized also that I needed to figure out how to feel good about my life, irrespective of my relationship to my sons. Not an easy task, but a real and essential one, and one I had been blind to when I was unconsciously hoping my sons could do it for me. Over a period of about four or five months, I worked intensively, examining my thinking and my self-talk, and reframing beliefs,

such as the one I just mentioned, that were negative and unconstructive. I managed to penetrate a whole network of misconceptions and negative conclusions about me. Although this was difficult and often painful work, I was encouraged because it was pretty exciting to see my mind changing. I began to reconstruct a more realistic view of my life and my relationship with my sons and with others. For one thing, I came to realize that my sons and I have become quite different people from who we were when we were all more closely bound together in earlier years. This is really no surprise when I consider it objectively, but I had never realized that before.

For another thing, I've come to the startling realization that maybe I can no longer define myself as a mother. The one role I felt I still had, I had given up being a mate, I had given up being a professional, being a horseback rider, a skier, I'm still a swimmer and a yogi, but given up quite a number of things as I've grown older. It came as a shock that maybe I am no longer a mother, at least in any functioning way. I wondered how I could get to believing my life had been worthwhile if my one mainstay, motherhood, no longer pertained. Of course, this identity crisis also brought up doubts about my Zen practice and why it had not been sufficient to sustain me through this.

Had I not been faithful enough, say, lazy, lacking commitment, belief? Yeah, yeah, maybe yeah. Why, after so many years of practice, was I still struggling in such a fundamental way? Or struggling again? Maybe I actually should have become a priest, or would I have failed at that too? So, the self-doubt drill. You might have had the experience of having a book, just the right book or just the right teaching, fall into your hands just when you need it most.

This has been happening to me in the past few months as I have been confronting these painful realities of my life and nature, and also as I've been preparing to be Shuso, which has been a powerful process in itself. The Rodney Smith book that I mentioned earlier is one of the books, but there have been several others, including even a novel about the mind, that really helped me get some insight into how our minds work. Rodney Smith says, as a way of reassuring me as I read it, the call of the Dharma is toward the difficult, not the comfortable. And a few pages later, an awakened life depends upon addressing the pain of being separated from those I love most.

Just in time, these sentences gave me solace. He said that it's pretty common for even long-term practitioners to get stuck, to fail, to push through and break out of the limitations of the ego and the mind. How it is because our mind is so invested in maintaining our sense of self that we feel separate from others. That is, it's the thought that we're separate and that alone that makes us separate. Our feeling separate has no more reality than that. So I began to think, well, maybe I'm not so disconnected. Again, Rodney Smith, speaking of renunciation in Dharma practice, says that what we must renounce in practice is a partial heart.

That's what keeps us from full realization or enlightenment or liberation. It's an incomplete embrace of the moment. I see now that my habit of hesitation has kept me from wholeheartedness a lot of times. Smith goes on to say that what prevents us from being wholly present in the moment is our competing intentions. Certainly being a person with many interests, I realize I've had many competing intentions in my life that have competed with my devotion to Zen practice. Competing intentions have been at the heart of my struggle about priesthood and perhaps also characteristic of my practice generally. I have often, though not always, had a partial heart. So even after 37 years of practice, this is probably a fundamental reason why I've struggled to fully trust my beliefs, as I've always wanted to.

I very much regret my partial heart. I'm even ashamed of it. And yet I recognize it is an essential aspect of myself. And therefore, it's what I must and do practice with. It is a condition of being me. Perhaps the essential pain. Rodney goes on to say, until there is complete dedication to being in the same place and same time as our body, our life is incomplete and irresolute. We must understand we are not needed anywhere but now.

And our only purpose for being is here. Spiritual fulfillment can be defined as a complete abiding in the here. So I ask myself, where am I now? I am here. I'm not with my sons and their families. In effect, or perhaps even by definition, I am not needed there. My life is here. Therefore, again, perhaps by definition, this is where I am needed.

Here is where I will find liberation. Only here. One who can save myself, the Buddha's admonition to us all. Not my sons, not anyone else. Of course, I've known this for years. But it's only now, when I've come to feel my vulnerability to old age, sickness, and death, that I have finally understood it with my heart. Through this crisis of identity this past year, through the hard work of therapy that I've done, through the wonderful books that I've found or that have found me when I most needed them. Through my sons leaving me when I could not understand that I had to leave them.

I think I finally understand what to do. It is by living my life wholeheartedly where I am, by continuing to learn and grow, that I will be able to die feeling my life has been worthwhile. And even though I continue to sense a hardcore resistance within me when I think about relinquishing my sons, I do believe now that by following my heart, I will find what I need to do. That is, by living in the present moment, I can live wholeheartedly. It's common to think that when we grow old, even if we're healthy, we just kind of fade away, lose interest and engagement in life. I had kind of expected this. But I'm here to tell you that life can get even more interesting. There is always more to learn and understand, and of course we know change never ceases.

Norman has said, we're fully alive until we're not. And maybe as Norman has encouraged me to believe, my sons will come closer sometime in the future when their journeys allow it. I don't count on that, but I will certainly be open and happy if that becomes a reality. But whatever happens, I feel I now understand that in order to live fullheartedly, which is to live in my body in the present, that's what I have. This recent experience of letting go of how things ought to be, just enough so I could see something different, has allowed me to see that my long-held preference that my sons relate to me in a way that makes me feel good about myself is the very thing that is preventing me from feeling good. Also, I think I understand something I didn't before. I'm thinking that maybe love flows mostly one way, from me to my sons, from my sons to their children.

My love for my sons doesn't come back directly to me as I've been expecting and hoping for, but it makes a big, wide circle. These shifts in my understanding have helped me to accept and choose the reality that is here, not the version that I had wished for. It thus relieved my suffering some. Being as hard-headed as I seem to have been all my life, always wanting things the way I would. I require a pretty major crisis in order to change. The last nine months, I have been working at changing my habitual, historical perceptions and beliefs. My work is not done. I have a ways to go before I no longer wish things could be different. But I am certain that I would not have been able to make any of this shift without Zazen and the calm center and suspension of the habitual thought that it offers.

I am grateful and thrilled, actually, that at my advancing age, my mind is capable of such an important shift. Although the struggle I've been having in my old age might be discouraging for you to hear, if you are looking forward to a peaceful decline, I hope you too will be encouraged that you can count on Zazen throughout your life to lead you where you need to go.
